statement: The system shall allow operators to supervise and control turbines from different vendors through one standardized communication method.
The system shall reliably transfer measurements, status, alarms, and commands between turbines, wind-farm controllers, and authorized applications.
The system shall preserve safe local turbine operation if communication is lost.
The system shall provide consistent access to plant data.
The system shall handle commands dependably under normal and degraded network conditions.
Only authorized parties shall be able to access the appropriate functions and data.
The communication system shall support remote supervision and control of wind turbines from different vendors.
The system shall ensure that local plant operation remains safe if communication is lost.
The turbine supervision workflow is fragmented.
Different turbine vendors provide their own interfaces and conventions.
Operators monitor data through vendor-specific systems or plant-level tools.
Commands are sent back through whatever channel the equipment supports.
Standardization is difficult in the current workflow.
The system shall provide a single standardized way to exchange measurements across turbines from different suppliers.
The system shall provide a single standardized way to exchange alarms across turbines from different suppliers.
The system shall provide a single standardized way to exchange status information across turbines from different suppliers.
The system shall provide a single standardized way to exchange commands across turbines from different suppliers.
The system shall provide a single standardized way to exchange settings across turbines from different suppliers.
The system shall not depend on each vendor’s custom solution for communication between operator applications and plant controllers.
The system shall improve reliability.
The system shall ensure clearer separation so that a communication problem does not interfere with the turbine’s safe local behavior.
Those are the main functions the system is aiming for.
The system shall restrict command sending and access to certain data to authorized operational applications and users.
The system shall provide traceability for commands and alarms.
The system shall support operators in knowing what happened and when.
The system shall provide authentication and authorization so that only approved applications and users can access or control the turbines.
The system shall protect communication against tampering or misuse.
The exact security mechanisms shall be aligned with the organisation's IT and operations policies.
Standardized data exchange shall be prioritized first.
Command and control shall be prioritized together with access control and security after standardized data exchange.
Reliability during communication failures shall be treated as critical.
Traceability shall be treated as secondary unless the team needs auditability for operations from day one.
The system shall allow supervisory and plant-level applications to read the same basic turbine information in a consistent way.
The system shall present measurements, operating status, alarms, and key plant data in the same way to the consuming system.
The system shall avoid requiring a separate integration for each turbine type.
The system shall support adding new turbines or applications later without redesigning the whole communication setup.
The system should standardize core operational data first.
The system should standardize active measurements such as power.
The system should standardize wind conditions.
The system should standardize rotor speed.
The system should standardize temperatures.
The system should standardize similar status values.
The system should standardize alarm and fault information.
Operators need these data continuously to supervise the farm and respond quickly to problems.
The system should standardize less time-critical plant data and detailed settings after the core operational data.
The first standardized scope should include a few basic control-related states.
The standardized control-related states should include whether a turbine is available.
The standardized control-related states should include whether a turbine is curtailed.
The standardized control-related states should include whether a turbine is stopped.
The first standardized scope should include a small set of environmental or site-level values when those values are commonly used for supervision.
The first standardized scope should avoid including too much detail unless that detail is needed across vendors.
Wind farm operators often run wind farms with turbines from several different manufacturers.
Each turbine vendor tends to have its own way of exchanging data and commands.
The system should reduce integration work caused by vendor-specific communication methods.
The system should make it easier to monitor the plant consistently from one operational environment.
The system should provide a standardized communication layer.
The standardized communication layer should carry measurements.
The standardized communication layer should carry alarms.
The standardized communication layer should carry status information.
The standardized communication layer should carry control commands between turbines or local controllers and authorized systems that need the information.
The plant should keep operating safely if the communication path fails.
The main users of the system are wind-farm operators and their authorized operational applications.
Turbine vendors or controller suppliers need to ensure their equipment can interface correctly with the standard.
The system has operations and maintenance personnel responsible for operations and maintenance.
The system shall support operations staff using supervisory or control applications as the main daily user group.
The system shall support a smaller technical user group, such as maintenance or engineering staff.
The system shall allow technical staff deeper access for diagnostics.
The system shall allow technical staff deeper access for configuration.
The system shall allow technical staff deeper access for verifying communication behavior.
The system shall restrict technical staff access so that it is more limited and controlled.
The system shall support vendor support users in exceptional cases.
The system shall not grant vendor support users broad routine access unless it is explicitly authorized.
The system shall support the core data types of measurements, status information, alarms, and commands.
In the wind-farm context, local control equipment may be referred to as a turbine controller or a wind-farm controller.
In the wind-farm context, central systems consuming the data may be referred to as a supervisory application or an operational application.
The system should consider availability, fail-safe operation, and authorized access as important behavior-related constraints.
The turbine shall send measurements and status updates continuously or at regular intervals to the authorized supervisory system.
When an alarm occurs, the system shall communicate the alarm quickly to the right application so the operator can assess it and decide whether action is needed.
Commands or setpoints shall be sent from an authorized system to the turbine or wind-farm controller.
Commands or setpoints shall be executed only if the local controller accepts them and the plant remains safe.
Weather changes should trigger more active communication.
Production curtailment should trigger more active communication.
Maintenance activities should trigger more active communication.
Abnormal turbine behavior should trigger more active communication.
A communication loss event should be visible to operators so they know the remote link has been interrupted.
The system shall support a phased rollout.
The system has no known hard external regulatory deadline at present.
After go-live, the system shall be maintainable mostly by the regular operations and IT teams rather than only by the original specialists.
The training approach should include short classroom-style training.
Interfaces should be consistent across vendors to reduce training effort.
The system shall provide contextual help for alarms.
The system shall prompt for confirmation before executing risky commands.
The system shall provide clear status feedback after an action is performed.
The system shall keep the workflow simple.
The ongoing support materials shall include a contact path for questions during the first months after rollout.
The system shall provide a clear audit trail for actions that could affect turbine availability or safety.
The contextual help shall use plain language and avoid too much technical detail.
The system shall warn when a command is unusual or outside normal operating patterns.
The system shall provide contextual help that groups related alarms or explains the likely cause when an operator is handling multiple turbines during a storm and receives a flood of alarms.
The system shall display a clear command result state as success, pending, or failed.
The system's contextual help shall explain alarm or control messages in operational terms rather than vendor language.
The system shall accommodate differences in each vendor's interface and data model.
The system shall provide adapters or gateways and perform extensive validation before switching any live turbines.
The system shall support parallel operation for a period so operators can compare outputs and confirm that nothing is lost during the transition.
The system shall use mapping layers to translate each vendor’s tags, alarms, and command structures into the standardized format.
The system shall keep raw source data traceable so that conversion can be verified for loss or misinterpretation.
The system shall perform automated reconciliation checks and test runs in a staging environment for critical values before going live.
The system shall include automated interface test suites and validation scripts.
The automated interface test suites and validation scripts shall compare source and target points, alarm codes, timestamps, and command acknowledgments.
The automated interface test suites and validation scripts shall flag mismatches for review before deployment.
If a discrepancy occurs, the system shall block cutover for the affected interface until the issue is corrected and re-tested.
The system shall maintain a persistent mapping record for every translated point, alarm, and command.
The mapping record shall include both the original vendor identifier and the standardized identifier.
The system shall display both the source and standardized sides in logs and the audit trail.
The system shall allow an engineer to navigate from a standardized event back to the source tag and view when and how it was transformed.
The system shall retain traceability for troubleshooting, compliance checks, and post-incident review.
The system shall allow users to start troubleshooting in the alarm or event view.
The system shall allow users to open related point details to see the original vendor tag.
The system shall allow users to view translation history in related point details.
The system shall allow users to view recent communication status in related point details.
The system shall provide a search or audit screen for troubleshooting and audits.
The search or audit screen shall allow filtering by turbine.
The search or audit screen shall allow filtering by vendor.
The search or audit screen shall allow filtering by time range.
The search or audit screen shall allow filtering by alarm type.
The search or audit screen shall allow users to pull the full trail without switching systems.
The interface shall make it easy to jump from the standardized record to the raw source details.
The system shall restrict access to raw source details to authorized users only.
The system shall use role-based access control so that operators can see the standardized operational view.
The system shall allow engineers and administrators to access deeper vendor-specific details.
The system shall require elevated approval or a second-person check for especially sensitive actions such as viewing raw mappings or exportable audit trails, depending on site policy.
The system shall log every access event so that users, viewed data, and access times can be reviewed later.
The system shall protect the plant and the data.
The system shall balance performance and validation when designing updates from the turbines.
The system shall support fast updates from the turbines.
The system shall avoid overloading the communication channels with heavy checking.
The system shall distinguish between functions that need immediate access and functions that can tolerate delays or extra approval.
The system shall be validated using functional testing.
The system shall be validated using failure-injection tests.
The system shall be validated using operator walkthroughs in a staging environment that resembles the real plant.
The system shall have an interface that is usable under time pressure.
The system shall receive sign-off from operations before deployment.
The system shall receive sign-off from engineering before deployment.
The system shall receive sign-off from cybersecurity before deployment.
Operations, safety, cybersecurity, and the vendor integration team shall each contribute to the formal review of conflicts during design.
The decision from the formal review shall be recorded against the risk.
During incidents, the control room or on-call operations lead shall make the immediate call.
Security and engineering shall support the incident response afterward so as not to delay a safe response.
The system shall reduce the complexity and cost of operating a mixed fleet.
The system shall standardize how vendors expose data and accept commands.
The system shall enable the control room and operational tools to work across turbines more consistently.
The system shall improve efficiency.
The system shall make training easier.
The system shall make maintenance easier.
The system shall provide better reliability in day-to-day operations.
The system shall handle alarms, measurements, and control actions in a common way even if a communication link or vendor system has issues.
The system shall support safer operations.
The system shall support more predictable operations.
The system shall reduce integration headaches.
The system shall reduce dependence on vendor-specific solutions.
The standardized communication system shall support both monitoring and control.
The system shall collect measurements, status, and alarms.
The system shall send commands and settings changes back to individual turbines or the wind-farm controller when authorized.
The control side shall be tightly controlled so that local safe operation is never put at risk if communication fails.
Remote commands or settings changes shall be allowed only when the turbine or farm controller is in a normal supervised operating state.
Remote commands or settings changes shall be allowed only when the operator is authenticated and authorized.
If the communication link is delayed, unstable, or lost, the system shall block or cancel remote actions rather than queue them for later delivery.
Local control at the turbine or farm level shall always take precedence for safe shutdown, protection, and any emergency action.
The system shall support remote supervision of a mix of wind farms with turbines from different manufacturers, including cases where different manufacturers are present within the same site.
The system shall support supervision from a central operations team.
The system shall support access for operators, maintenance staff, and authorized external parties such as service providers and vendor support.
The system shall enforce different access levels so that access is not the same for everyone.
The system shall cover normal production sites.
The system shall cover maintenance situations.
The system shall cover troubleshooting situations.
The system shall cover alarm response situations.
The system shall allow remote viewing of a specific turbine or a group of turbines.
The remote supervision system shall initially cover selected plants.
The initial scope shall prioritize sites with mixed vendors or sites where remote operations provide the most value.
The remote supervision system shall not include every turbine in the fleet on day one.
The remote supervision system shall be designed so that its scope can be expanded later without redesigning the system.
Some sites shall support supervision only.
Some sites shall require full command capability depending on the local setup and operating agreement.
Operators shall be able to monitor the fleet.
Operators shall be able to acknowledge alarms.
Operators shall be able to issue the normal operational commands they are trained for.
Maintenance staff shall have access to diagnostics.
Maintenance staff shall have access to some configuration functions.
Maintenance staff shall have access to some test functions.
Maintenance staff shall only access assets they are responsible for.
Maintenance staff shall usually access assets during an agreed maintenance window.
External service providers shall have the most limited access.
External service providers shall mostly have read-only access.
External service providers shall mostly have tightly scoped service actions.
Central operations shall retain control over higher-risk commands.
Central operations shall retain control over access permissions.
Central operations shall retain control over changes that affect multiple turbines or site-wide behavior.
The system shall use common naming and definitions.
People can act only within their assigned assets and role scope.
Anything that crosses into site-wide or multi-turbine impact requires central operations approval.
If a command could affect other turbines, the farm controller, or a safety-critical state, the system shall treat it as restricted even if the person has access to the individual turbine.
The system shall check both asset ownership and command impact before allowing a command.
The system shall block anything that exceeds the user's authorization.
Delayed or interrupted commands should generally be blocked or canceled rather than recovered later.
A very low-risk action may be allowed if it can be verified as still valid before execution.
Any allowance for delayed or interrupted commands must be very tightly controlled and probably limited to specific cases.
Commands that could change operating state should not be executed after a link interruption.
Commands that could affect safety behavior should not be executed after a link interruption.
Commands that could affect multiple assets should not be executed after a link interruption.
Access to logs and monitoring data should be restricted by role.
Only authorized operations and maintenance personnel may view detailed logs.
Authorized personnel should only see the information they need for their work.
The system should retain enough history for troubleshooting.
The system should retain enough history for audit purposes.
The system should retain enough history for incident review.
Sharing logs and monitoring data outside the authorized group should be controlled.
Logs and monitoring data shared outside the authorized group should be anonymized or redacted where possible.
Information that exposes operator actions or sensitive asset details should be treated as protected information.
Retention periods and sharing rules should be defined with security and compliance.
The system shall integrate with some existing vendor supervision systems instead of replacing everything at once.
The system shall support a mixed fleet where not every site is at the same lifecycle stage.
The scope of vendor supervision systems shall be confirmed site by site.
The scope of connected assets beyond the turbines shall be confirmed site by site.
The system shall account for connected assets beyond the turbines, including farm controllers and existing local SCADA components.
The interface layer shall map or translate different vendor tag names, data models, and alarm codes.
The system rollout shall support a period during which old and new interfaces run side by side.
Log and monitoring data should be available outside the core operations and maintenance group only when there is a clear operational need.
Incident investigation is an example of a clear operational need for access to log and monitoring data outside the core operations and maintenance group.
Performance analysis is an example of a clear operational need for access to log and monitoring data outside the core operations and maintenance group.
Vendor support for a specific fault is an example of a clear operational need for access to log and monitoring data outside the core operations and maintenance group.
When log and monitoring data is shared outside the core operations and maintenance group for an operational need, access should be limited to the minimum necessary data.
When log and monitoring data is shared outside the core operations and maintenance group for an operational need, access should be time-bound where possible.
When log and monitoring data is shared outside the core operations and maintenance group for an operational need, access should be approved by the person responsible for operations or security.
External support should not receive broad access to log and monitoring data by default.
Sensitive identifiers and operator actions should be masked unless there is a strong reason to reveal them.
The receiving application shall treat data with missing, delayed, or inconsistent validity information as suspect and shall not use it for control decisions unless its validity can be confirmed.
For monitoring or reporting, the receiving application may store or display such data.
The receiving application shall clearly mark stored or displayed data as uncertain, delayed, or incomplete so operators know it cannot be fully trusted.
If timestamp or quality information is inconsistent, the application should reject the value rather than silently assume it is correct.
The system shall support whatever interface types are practical for the different vendors and the authorized operational applications.
The system shall use a mix of standardized industrial interfaces rather than a single protocol everywhere.
The system shall accept some proprietary vendor formats at first for legacy sites.
The system shall accept proprietary vendor formats only where there is no feasible alternative.
The system shall preferably place proprietary vendor formats behind an adapter layer.
Commands initiated by manual operator actions, scheduled tasks, and automated triggers shall be treated differently.
Manual operator actions shall require explicit authorization.
Automated commands shall fire only when the triggering condition is unambiguous.
Automated commands shall be blocked if key inputs are stale.
Extra approval shall be required for anything that restarts equipment after a trip.
The system shall comply with applicable industry and regulatory requirements related to safety, cybersecurity, and grid operations.
The system shall be designed for compliance from the outset rather than adding compliance later.
There may be jurisdiction-specific rules that change both approval and retention.
The applicable regulator and market rules for each deployment site must be confirmed before finalizing the workflow.
Some deployment sites shall require local approval chains for certain commands.
Some deployment sites shall require tighter operating limits during specific grid conditions.
The system shall assume that jurisdiction-specific overrides can exist.
A local regulator or market rule may require longer retention for audit records.
The first approval shall usually be obtained from the site operator or control room.
The system should make it difficult for a new operator to make mistakes.
The system should allow new users to perform only low-risk actions until they have been trained and approved.
The interface should validate inputs before anything can be sent.
The control path shall be treated more strictly than monitoring data.
The system may tolerate stale measurements to some extent.
Allowable delay thresholds shall be defined per operating mode.
The system shall allow a command to proceed only if the stale data is within a short, defined freshness window and the command is low risk.
The system shall allow an interface type only if it is proven compatible with the vendor’s turbine or controller and approved for the specific authorized application at the site.
The adapter shall be treated as a high-risk boundary.
The adapter may buffer traffic if buffering is strictly limited to preserving the approved message flow and does not change the meaning of the command or measurement.
The adapter may perform a small amount of transformation only if the transformation is deterministic and fully documented.
The system's design shall account for applicable internal security policies or national grid and safety rules, if they apply.
The requirements team shall verify the applicable legal or standards compliance set with the compliance and cybersecurity teams.
Applicable rules shall dictate approved encryption methods for the adapter.
Applicable rules shall dictate minimum log retention for the adapter.
Applicable rules shall dictate where the adapter is allowed to sit on the network.
National critical infrastructure cybersecurity rules are expected to be a main driver governing the adapter’s communication handling.
Utility or grid-operator connection requirements are expected to be a main driver governing the adapter’s communication handling.
The company’s own IT and OT security policies are expected to be a main driver governing the adapter’s communication handling.
Applicable requirements are expected to constrain which encryption algorithms are approved for the adapter.
Applicable requirements are expected to constrain how long logs must be kept.
Applicable requirements are expected to constrain whether the adapter must be placed in an OT segment or a screened zone rather than directly on the control network.
Queuing or retrying is acceptable only if the message remains valid after a short delay and there is no risk of acting on stale state.
Any queue or retry behavior shall be bounded so that it cannot build up indefinitely.
If the adapter drops traffic, it shall log the message type, source, time, and reason for rejection.
If the adapter drops traffic, it shall log whether the failure was data-related, authentication-related, or an adapter fault.
The adapter shall escalate to the operator when the condition affects availability or could block an authorized control action.
The log shall identify whether the dropped message was telemetry, a status update, an alarm, or an actual control command.
If the dropped message was a control action, the log shall capture the intended target turbine or controller and whether the command was safety-related or routine.
The log shall not expose unnecessary payload details.
The log shall record operator-visible context such as an active incident or a degraded communications state.
The site access mode shall depend on the site's operational agreement and the maturity of the vendor integration.
Full command capability shall be reserved for sites where the communication path, responsibilities, and safety handling are agreed and tested end to end.
The fleet scope shall be noted as tentative for now.
There is no confirmed list of plants or site types yet.
The list of plants or site types shall not be locked down before the operational teams and the owners have agreed to it.
For new integrations, the system shall treat open, well-documented industrial protocols as the default.
The system shall not name a fixed list of preferred protocols until vendor support has been checked at the selected sites.
A protocol shall not be accepted if it is too opaque, too unstable, or cannot be mapped safely to the required measurements, status, alarms, and commands.
For the first rollout, direct support shall be required for anything that affects safe operation.
For the first rollout, direct support shall be required for alarms.
For the first rollout, direct support shall be required for essential status.
For the first rollout, direct support shall be required for any command that can start turbine behavior.
For the first rollout, direct support shall be required for any command that can stop turbine behavior.
For the first rollout, direct support shall be required for any command that can change turbine behavior.
Limited coverage through an adapter layer may be accepted for non-critical measurements.
Limited coverage through an adapter layer may be accepted for convenience data.
Limited coverage through an adapter layer may be accepted only if the missing parts are clearly outside the initial operational need.
Limited coverage through an adapter layer may be accepted only if it does not weaken supervision.
If the adapter cannot represent a required item without ambiguity, the site or protocol combination shall wait rather than be forced into the pilot.
The system shall operate in supervision-only mode when the local operator or owner has not approved remote control.
The system shall operate in supervision-only mode when there is not enough confidence in the command path and safety handling.
The system shall operate in supervision-only mode when the site is still being commissioned.
The system shall operate in supervision-only mode when the vendor integration is incomplete.
The system shall operate in supervision-only mode when regulatory or contractual restrictions limit who may issue commands.
The system shall require an explicit operating agreement before full command capability is allowed.
The system shall require validated command safety checks before full command capability is allowed.
The system shall require confirmation that the local fallback behavior is independent and remains safe if communication fails before full command capability is allowed.
The site shall comply with the applicable safety rules before moving to remote commands.
The site shall comply with grid or market operator requirements before moving to remote commands.
The site shall comply with the contractual permissions agreed between the owner and the local operator before moving to remote commands.
The site shall conform to the relevant communication and control standards used for turbine and substation operation before moving to remote commands.
A documented risk assessment shall show that command handling will not compromise local safe shutdown or recovery before moving to remote commands.
The system shall remain supervision-only when the legal arrangement does not permit remote actuation.
The system shall remain supervision-only when the operator decides the site's risk profile is too high for remote control.
The monitoring display shall allow operators to see that something is coming in.
If the issue cannot be explained cleanly, the value shall be rejected outright.
The system shall use bounded retry only when the translation failure appears transient.
Any bounded retry for a transient translation failure shall be limited to a short, defined window.
The system shall escalate to an operator if the same translation failure repeats.
The system shall escalate to an operator if an unsafe translation event affects a safety-related command or alarm.
The system shall escalate to an operator if the retry window expires without success.
The system shall keep an uncertain value visible if it still helps operators understand the site situation, especially for monitoring trends or comparing with other data.
The system shall hide or reject an uncertain value when the uncertainty is so high that it could mislead an operator into taking action.
The system shall reject any value tied to alarms or commands unless it can be confirmed as valid.
